lessons.title: ಸೋಮವಾರ to ಭಾನುವಾರ — the Sanskrit week
lessons.headword: ಸೋಮವಾರ ಮಂಗಳವಾರ ಬುಧವಾರ ಗುರುವಾರ ಶುಕ್ರವಾರ ಶನಿವಾರ ಭಾನುವಾರ
lessons.gloss: the seven weekdays — fully Sanskritic, like Hindi, but Sunday uses a DIFFERENT sun-name

segments.text: Unlike Tamil and Malayalam, Kannada's week is built entirely from Sanskrit — the same recipe as Hindi's. But even here, one day picks a different Sanskrit word than Hindi does.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: The pattern: [deity] + ವಾರ, "day"

utterances: Kannada: ಸೋಮವಾರ (Somavāra). deity/planet: Moon (Soma). day: Monday.
Kannada: ಮಂಗಳವಾರ (Maṅgaḷavāra). deity/planet: Mars (Maṅgala). day: Tuesday.
Kannada: ಬುಧವಾರ (Budhavāra). deity/planet: Mercury (Budha). day: Wednesday.
Kannada: ಗುರುವಾರ (Guruvāra). deity/planet: Jupiter (Guru/Bṛhaspati). day: Thursday.
Kannada: ಶುಕ್ರವಾರ (Śukravāra). deity/planet: Venus (Śukra). day: Friday.
Kannada: ಶನಿವಾರ (Śanivāra). deity/planet: Saturn (Śani). day: Saturday.
Kannada: ಭಾನುವಾರ (Bhānuvāra). deity/planet: the Sun (Bhānu, "light, splendor"). day: Sunday.

segments.text: Five of these are identical in shape to Hindi's — same deity, same ‑vāra/ ‑vār ending. Sunday is the interesting exception: where Hindi says रविवार (Ravivār, from Ravi, "sun"), Kannada says ಭಾನುವಾರ (Bhānuvāra), built on a different Sanskrit word for the sun — Bhānu, "light, splendor," rather than Ravi. Sanskrit has many names for the sun, and different languages downstream picked different ones for their week.

segments.instruction: "Somavāra, Maṅgaḷavāra, Budhavāra, Guruvāra, Śukravāra, Śanivāra" — Monday through Saturday
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "Somavāra, Maṅgaḷavāra, Budhavāra, Guruvāra, Śukravāra, Śanivāra" — Monday through Saturday]

segments.instruction: the contrast — Hindi says Ravivāra (Ravi), Kannada says Bhānuvāra (Bhānu) — two different Sanskrit sun-names
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the contrast — Hindi says Ravivāra (Ravi), Kannada says Bhānuvāra (Bhānu) — two different Sanskrit sun-names]

segments.text: What ending does every Kannada weekday share, and where's it from? (‑ವಾರ -vāra, Sanskrit "day.") Which day differs from Hindi's version, and how? (Sunday — Kannada's Bhānuvāra ("light") uses a different Sanskrit sun-name than Hindi's Ravivār ("Ravi").)

lessons.title: ತ (ta) — one character, met inside words you already say
lessons.gloss: the single character ತ — recognised inside words you already say

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script you'll notice: ತ and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Before the new one: ◌ಿ — what does it do?
One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
ತ — ta.
It is a consonant, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an a already in it. So it is not t, it is ta.
You already say these, and every one of them has ತ (ta) somewhere inside it:
ಸಂತೋಷ santōṣa — joy / pleased to meet you.
ಹೋಗಿ ಬರುತ್ತೇನೆ hōgi baruttēne — goodbye (lit. "I'll go and come back").
ಮತ್ತೆ ಸಿಗೋಣ matte sigōṇa — we'll meet again.
ಮಾತನಾಡು mātanāḍu — to speak.

blocks.title: Writing: ತ — copy what you see

segments.text: Put your pen on ತ (ta) and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

This book does not yet tell you where to start the character or which way to travel. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.

segments.instruction: at these words, and find ತ (ta) in the ones that have it
segments.source: [YOU LOOK: at these words, and find ತ in the ones that have it]

segments.text: ಸಂತೋಷ, ಹೋಗಿ ಬರುತ್ತೇನೆ, ನಮಸ್ಕಾರ.

segments.instruction: ತ three times, saying ta as you finish each one
segments.source: [YOU TRACE: ತ three times, saying *ta* as you finish each one]

segments.instruction: back at any page of this chapter and find ತ (ta) once more
segments.source: [YOU LOOK: back at any page of this chapter and find ತ once more]

segments.text: Which character is this — ತ? What sound does it carry? (ta.) Name one word you already say that contains it.

lessons.title: ◌ೊ — one character, met inside words you already say
lessons.gloss: the single character ೊ — recognised inside words you already say

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script you'll notice: ◌ೊ and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Before the new one: ಳ — what does it do?
One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
It is a vowel sign. It is not a letter and never stands alone: it attaches to a consonant and replaces the a built into it with o. Replaces, not adds — the a is gone.
You already say these, and every one of them has ◌ೊ somewhere inside it:
ನನಗೆ ಕನ್ನಡ ಗೊತ್ತು nanage kannaḍa gottu — 'I know Kannada'.
Put your pen on ◌ೊ and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

This book does not yet tell you where to start the character or which way to travel. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.

segments.instruction: at these words, and find ◌ೊ in the ones that have it
segments.source: [YOU LOOK: at these words, and find ◌ೊ in the ones that have it]

segments.text: ನಮಸ್ಕಾರ.

segments.instruction: ◌ೊ three times, saying o as you finish each one
segments.source: [YOU TRACE: ◌ೊ three times, saying *o* as you finish each one]

segments.instruction: back at any page of this chapter and find ◌ೊ once more
segments.source: [YOU LOOK: back at any page of this chapter and find ◌ೊ once more]

segments.text: Which character is this — ◌ೊ? What vowel does it put on the consonant it attaches to — and what does it take off? (Puts o on; takes the built-in a off.) Name one word you already say that contains it.
